passage:
I'm Yogesh, site supervisor for twenty years. Swati joined us as a junior engineer eighteen months ago.
Tuesday morning, the concrete truck was waiting to pour the third-floor slab. Swati walked the formwork, stopped halfway, and frowned. "Hold the pour. Something's off." She couldn't say what.
The truck driver grumbled. I didn't argue; I've seen that look on older engineers. She got down on her knees and checked the props one by one. Near the corner, one support had been set on a loose brick instead of a proper base plate.
Afterwards I asked her how she knew. "I didn't," she said. "It just looked different from the hundred slabs I've walked. So I checked."
Maybe it was the angle, maybe a shadow. I can't say for sure. But the pour went ahead an hour late, and safe.

qa.q: What was the corner support set on?
qa.a: A loose brick instead of a proper base plate.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling before she could explain it?
qa.a: Swati felt uneasy that something was off, because the formwork looked different from the hundred slabs she had walked.

qa.q: What did Swati do with the feeling that made it useful?
qa.a: She treated it as a cue to check, holding the pour and inspecting the props one by one, instead of ignoring it or acting on it blindly.

qa.q: How does Yogesh see Swati's hunch?
qa.a: Yogesh recognises the look from older engineers and trusts it enough to wait, while admitting to not knowing exactly what she noticed.

grounding: A supervisor watches a young woman engineer sense a problem from experience before she can name it, and use the feeling as a cue to check.

passage:
March. In her third week on the surgical ward, Rituparna noted Mr Mohit in bed two as "comfortable". An hour later, the senior nurse spotted what she hadn't: he had gone quiet and pale. Rituparna replayed it all evening at home.
November. Bed six, Divyansh, a college student two days after surgery. His readings were normal. But Rituparna paused at the foot of the bed. He was too still; he wasn't scrolling his phone the way he had yesterday. She couldn't have named it. She checked everything again, found one reading edging the wrong way, and called the doctor.
The next morning, the senior nurse asked what had made her look twice. Rituparna thought about it. "Hundreds of patients, I suppose. He just didn't look like someone getting better. So I checked instead of guessing."

qa.q: What had Divyansh stopped doing that he did the day before?
qa.a: Scrolling his phone.

qa.q: What did Rituparna feel at the foot of bed six?
qa.a: Rituparna felt uneasy that something was wrong, though the readings were normal and she couldn't yet name it; he didn't look like someone getting better.

qa.q: Why was checking again and calling the doctor the right use of her hunch?
qa.a: The feeling alone wasn't proof, so she used it as a cue to look closer, found a reading moving the wrong way, and brought in the right person.

qa.q: How might the senior nurse see Rituparna's growth since March?
qa.a: In March the senior nurse had to catch what she missed; by November she caught it herself, which would be very reassuring to see.

grounding: Over months, a young nurse builds a sense that something is wrong from hundreds of patients and learns to treat it as a cue to check.

passage:
Pradeep, before your first night route, let me tell you about Gauri. She joined my depot when I was the manager there, one of our youngest drivers, maybe twenty-four.
In her second year she was driving the ghat road one foggy night. Nothing on the dashboard. The engine sounded fine to any passenger. But she pulled into a lay-by and switched off. "Siddharth Sir," she told me on the phone, "it sounds a little wrong. I can't say how."
The mechanic came. A fan belt was fraying, about to go.
Later she said it was the hundreds of trips on that road; her ears knew what normal was. But she never just trusted the feeling. She always stopped and checked.
Your ears will learn too. Until then, and even after, when something feels wrong, you check.

qa.q: What did the mechanic find on Gauri's bus?
qa.a: A fan belt that was fraying, about to go.

qa.q: What did Gauri feel was wrong on the ghat road that night?
qa.a: Gauri felt uneasy because the engine sounded a little wrong, though nothing showed on the dashboard and she couldn't say how.

qa.q: What habit is Siddharth passing on to Pradeep?
qa.a: When something feels wrong, stop and check, both now and later, once experience has trained the ears.

qa.q: How might Gauri's passengers have felt if the belt had snapped on the ghat road?
qa.a: Frightened and stranded in fog on a steep road; her stop spared them that, even if the delay annoyed some.

grounding: A retired depot manager recalls a young woman driver who sensed an engine fault from hundreds of trips and treated the feeling as a cue to check.

passage: The monsoon ferry to Divar was already ten minutes late, and the skipper, Hemant, wanted to go before the next squall. Shraddha, twenty-five, the ferry's engineer for two years, stood by the engine hatch and frowned. The rumble sounded... off. Not louder, not quieter. Just wrong, somehow. "It's running," Hemant called. "Let's move." "Give me four minutes," she said. "I can't tell you why yet." Omkar, the deckhand, rolled his eyes and held the rope. Rain was coming sideways. Shraddha climbed down with her torch and went along the lines she had checked hundreds of times. Near the filter, a small wet shine: a hairline crack in the fuel pipe. She showed Hemant. He stopped arguing. They radioed for the spare ferry, and forty passengers waited under the shed, grumbling, but dry and safe.

qa.q: What did Shraddha find near the filter?
qa.a: A small wet shine: a hairline crack in the fuel pipe.

qa.q: Why did Shraddha ask for four minutes even though she couldn't say why?
qa.a: Shraddha felt uneasy because, after hundreds of checks, the engine's rumble sounded wrong to her, and she trusted that unease enough to look before sailing.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference here, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Checking the lines despite pressure to leave, because it turned a vague feeling into evidence before anyone was put at risk.

qa.q: How might the forty passengers have felt waiting under the shed?
qa.a: They were annoyed at the delay, but they likely would have felt differently if they had known about the cracked fuel pipe.

grounding: A young woman engineer senses something wrong before she can name it, from hundreds of checks, and treats the feeling as a cue to inspect.

passage: At the Jayanagar branch of the bank, Pema, twenty-five, had counted notes at the cash counter for three years. On a busy Friday a customer handed her a stack for deposit. Halfway through, her fingers paused on one note. It felt too smooth, maybe. Or too light. She couldn't say exactly. Her first thought was, you're tired, keep going. Instead she set it aside. "One moment, please." She called her senior, Varun, over and held the note under the counter lamp and the checking machine. The machine beeped red. Varun nodded slowly. "Good catch. What told you?" Pema shook her head. "Nothing I could explain. It just didn't feel like the others." Varun smiled. "That's what thousands of notes do. You were right to check, not just trust it."

qa.q: Where did Pema work, and for how long?
qa.a: At the Jayanagar branch of the bank, counting notes at the cash counter for three years.

qa.q: What was going on in Pema's mind when her fingers paused on the note?
qa.a: She noticed a vague sense that the note was different, doubted herself as tired, and then decided the feeling was worth checking.

qa.q: Why was setting the note aside the right step rather than simply accusing anyone?
qa.a: It let her test the hunch with the machine and her senior, so the decision rested on evidence, not just a feeling.

qa.q: How does Varun see Pema's feeling about the note?
qa.a: Varun sees it as a skill built from handling thousands of notes, and values that she checked it rather than trusting it blindly.

grounding: A young bank worker senses a note is wrong before she can explain why, from years of practice, and treats the feeling as a cue to check.
